title: Does an Executable Generate–Validate–Repair Loop Reduce Semantic Failures in LLM‑Generated NetOps Changes?
abstract: We report a fully preregistered paired experiment (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) that tested whether inserting an executable emulator validator into a generate→validate→repair pipeline (guarded) reduces semantic/network-level failures versus an LLM-only suggestion workflow (baseline). The deterministic paired design used N=120 intent→configuration tasks (40 per topology class: edge, core, leaf–spine). A single shared initial candidate per task was generated by gpt-5-mini (model_calls_used = 120). A deterministic emulator validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) applied intent-constraint and workflow-policy checks and could trigger ≤1 repair only when validator.violation_count>0. Outcomes: baseline success = 120/120 (1.00); guarded success = 120/120 (1.00). Contingency: n_11=120, n_10=0, n_01=0, n_00=0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; paired-difference estimate = 0.00; bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed=1729). Validator traces show repair_applied = false for all guarded episodes. We expand preregistered methodology, provide per-topology diagnostics, explain the statistical degeneracy, document execution accounting and contamination controls, and contextualize limitations and reproducibility using archived artifacts.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) can translate natural-language intent into vendor-style configuration commands, promising faster NetOps workflows. However, plausibly worded configuration suggestions can violate workflow invariants (for example, changing MTU without a required shutdown, or conducting an uplink switchover in the wrong order), producing semantic failures that only appear when changes are applied to network state. Prior literature therefore promotes integrating verification, emulation/digital twins, or veto layers into LLM-driven NetOps pipelines so generated candidates are checked and, if necessary, repaired before enactment.

This study asks a focused, preregistered mechanistic question: does adding an executable emulator validator (with a single-step repair budget) reduce emulator-observed semantic failures when compared to presenting the same generated candidate without validation? To answer this we used a paired, shared-generation design where each task produced one shared initial candidate (generation performed once per pair) and that identical candidate was evaluated under two conditions: baseline (LLM-only suggestion) and guarded (generate→validate→repair). By fixing generator output we isolate the incremental effect of validation/repair. The preregistration, execution accounting, validator traces, and analysis artifacts are archived and referenced below; key run statistics are reported in Results.
sections.related_work:
Closed-loop, executable benchmarks have recently emerged as essential tools for assessing operational reliability of LLM-driven NetOps because text-only correctness metrics miss semantic network-level failures. NetConfArena and contemporaneous executable testbeds evaluate agentic behavior in emulation; generate→validate→repair architectures have been proposed and empirically evaluated at prototype scale to reduce semantic errors in constrained scenarios. Survey and architecture papers emphasize guardrails (veto layers, canaries, translation-to-formal-model) as practical measures for agentic NetOps.

Our experiment complements prior work by holding the generator fixed and asking a different question: for identical generated candidates, can a validator/repair stage improve closed-loop outcomes? That isolation is distinct from prior multi-component end-to-end comparisons where generator variance and validator effects are conflated. The design therefore contributes a narrowly scoped but mechanistically clear test to the literature on verifier-augmented LLM NetOps workflows. The archived evidence-synthesis in the preregistration documents the literature leads that motivated the study.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and design: The study was preregistered (CNSM2026-A-prereg-v1) and frozen before execution. The preregistration specified a paired-binary design with exactly N=120 distinct intent→configuration tasks, deterministically assigned into three topology classes (40 tasks each: edge, core, leaf–spine). Each task produced one shared initial candidate generated by the declared model (gpt-5-mini) and used by both conditions. The guarded pipeline could invoke at most one repair and only if the deterministic emulator validator reported validator.violation_count>0. The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline evaluated with an exact two‑sided McNemar test; the preregistered power target was an absolute reduction of 0.15.

Generation and pairing semantics: To isolate validator/repair effects we used shared_initial_generation semantics: stage_counts in the execution manifest record shared_initial_generation = 120 and provider-call accounting shows model_calls_used = 120. The preregistration field independent_condition_generation=false enforced identical generator outputs across conditions. The archived execution/model_configuration.json records declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini" and other request parameters. Provider-call audit (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json) shows hosted_model_call_event_count = 120, cache_miss_count = 120 and no cross-condition cache reuse.

Validator and repair semantics: The guarded pipeline used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version = 5.0). The validator implements intent-constraint and workflow-policy checks expressed in the task payloads (for example: must_be_down_for_fields, make-before-break, final_group_constraints). For each episode the validator emits a structured validator_trace containing validation_before, validation_after, parsed_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, violation_count, violation_codes, and repair_applied flag. The preregistered repair policy applied at most one repair per guarded episode and only when violation_count > 0; repair_provider_trace artifacts are saved when a repair is executed. In this run every guarded validator_trace recorded violation_count = 0 and repair_applied = false; consequently no repair_provider_trace files exist in the archive.

Statistical procedures and degeneracy rationale: The confirmatory test is the exact two‑sided McNemar on paired binary outcomes (pass/fail). Complementary reporting includes the paired-difference estimate and a bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval (bootstrap_resamples = 10,000; bootstrap_seed = 1729; these parameters and the completed analysis event are recorded in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl). When an empirical paired contingency table has zero discordant pairs (n_10 = n_01 = 0), every bootstrap resample of the observed pairs reproduces the same concordant outcomes, producing a degenerate bootstrap distribution and a zero-width percentile CI. The archive therefore contains a valid but degenerate CI reflecting the observed ceiling outcome rather than numerical error.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and descriptive outcomes: The execution manifest reports planned_episode_count = 240, completed_episode_count = 240, failed_episode_count = 0, and model_calls_used = 120. analysis/condition_summary.csv shows baseline: 120 successes, 0 failures (success_rate = 1.0) and guarded: 120 successes, 0 failures (success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is:
- n_11 = 120 (both success),
- n_10 = 0 (guarded success only),
- n_01 = 0 (baseline success only),
- n_00 = 0 (both fail).

Confirmatory inference: With zero discordant pairs the exact two‑sided McNemar p-value equals 1.0. The paired-difference estimate = 0.00. The preregistered bootstrap percentile 95% CI computed with 10,000 resamples (seed = 1729) returned [0.00, 0.00]; the CI is degenerate because resampling the observed table reproduces identical paired outcomes in every resample. These exact values are recorded in analysis/results.json and in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl.

Per-topology diagnostics: Tasks were deterministically assigned 40 per topology class. Aggregated per-topology successes from the archived scoring JSONs are:
- Edge (40 tasks): baseline = 40/40; guarded = 40/40.
- Core (40 tasks): baseline = 40/40; guarded = 40/40.
- Leaf–spine (40 tasks): baseline = 40/40; guarded = 40/40.
These counts are supported by execution/task_manifest.jsonl entries and the per-episode scoring artifacts under execution/scoring/ (representative examples: task-000001, task-000002, task-000003 JSONs included in the archive).

Representative validator traces and example episodes: Representative scoring JSONs (for example, execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json and the corresponding baseline file) show normalized_response equal to normalized_reference_answer, parsed_command_count equal to required_command_count, validator_trace.validation_after.valid = true, and validator_trace.repair_applied = false. The included examples also show difficulty metadata (required_command_count, dependency_rule_count, level) that permit stratified diagnostics and permit future researchers to reproduce the validation logic applied to each task.

Contamination, missingness, and reconciliation: analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty (no contamination flags). analysis/missingness_summary.csv reports complete_pairs = 120 and zero technical/instrumentation exclusions. analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json confirms consistent episode accounting and provider-call audit (hosted_model_call_event_count = 120, no failed_hosted_model_call_event_count). No preregistered deviations or exclusions occurred.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation of the ceiling outcome: The paired shared-generation design intentionally isolates the validator/repair stage by presenting identical generated candidates to both conditions. In this run gpt-5-mini produced a set of shared candidates that universally satisfied the deterministic emulator's intent constraints and workflow policies, producing a concordant-success ceiling (n_11=120). Under these conditions the guarded pipeline could not exercise repair behavior and therefore could not produce an observable reduction in emulator-observed semantic failures versus baseline. The exact McNemar p=1.0 and degenerate bootstrap CI reflect this observed ceiling.

Methodological implications and boundaries of inference: The experiment answers a precise mechanistic question — whether a validator/repair stage improves outcomes for identical generator outputs — and in this task bank and generator/prompting configuration the answer is "no effect" because the generator produced only valid candidates. This narrow null result should not be interpreted to imply that validators are unnecessary in operational deployments. Generator variance, prompt perturbations, alternative model families, adversarial inputs, or production heterogeneity can produce invalid candidates; in those settings a validator/repair subsystem could be decisive.

Design lessons for future confirmatory tests: The preregistration targeted an absolute reduction of 0.15 with N=120 under an assumed baseline failure rate ≈0.40. That assumption was violated here because the curated task bank elicited zero baseline failures; the result therefore rendered the confirmatory test uninformative for the originally targeted effect size. To measure practical repair utility in future work we recommend (all permitted by the archived artifacts): (1) allow independent per-condition generation to expose generation variance; (2) expand repair budget to multiple iterations; (3) test multiple generator models and explicit prompt perturbations; and (4) employ more production-rooted, multi-vendor task corpora. The current archived task_manifest includes difficulty and dependency metadata that support stratified follow-up analyses along these dimensions.

Operational and reproducibility implications: Even when unused, a deterministic validator that emits structured traces (what rule passed/failed, which fields were touched, and whether a repair was applied) supports operator auditability and post-hoc incident analysis. The archived provider-call audit and deterministic reconciliation artifacts show how to instrument runs for accountable operation and independent verification. Because the experiment and all artifacts (model configuration, raw responses, scoring JSONs, pair-level manifests, and analysis outputs) are archived, future researchers can replay the exact run, alter pairing semantics, or substitute alternative models under an identical harness.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired experiment (N=120) comparing an executable generate→validate→repair pipeline to an LLM-only workflow under a deterministic harness and a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini). All 120 shared initial candidates passed the deterministic emulator validator, producing n_11=120 and a paired-difference estimate of 0.00 (exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.00], 10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). The result documents a ceiling effect on this curated synthetic task bank and highlights that a shared-generation paired design can mask validator/repair benefits that would emerge when generator outputs sometimes violate intent constraints. Our principal contribution is methodological: we demonstrate how a preregistered, artifact-rich paired design cleanly isolates validator/repair effects and we show how deterministic archival artifacts support reproducible failure analyses and informed design choices for future comparisons.

limitations: Confirmatory scope: results are narrowly scoped to the preregistered synthetic task set, a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini), and a frozen prompting strategy; generalization to production heterogeneity is limited.
Synthetic task provenance: tasks were synthetic/deterministic and may underrepresent noisy, adversarial, or multi-vendor production incidents; external validity to live networks is constrained.

Shared-generation design: using a single shared initial generation per paired task isolates validator/repair efficacy but precludes detection of generation-variance effects; this choice contributed to the ceiling outcome and limits inference about repair utility on independently generated invalid outputs.

Validator fidelity: the deterministic emulator/validator is reproducible but simplifies heterogeneity present in multi-vendor, partially observable production environments; some real-world failure modes may not be exposed.

Statistical ceiling: baseline success reached 100% on the tested task bank, violating the preregistered power assumptions (targeted absolute reduction = 0.15) and rendering the McNemar confirmatory test uninformative for the originally targeted effect size.
